rows.got: FOUND. Samuel Sneyd, born 13 March 1811, baptised 28 April 1811 — father Samuel, mother Elizabeth, abode Hanley. The tree names exactly those parents. A sister, Mary, follows in 1814 with the father's occupation recorded: SERVANT. Every previous search had gone to Madeley because that is where the disproved Keele graft pointed.

rows.src: FreeREG — Madeley All Saints, the 1769 marriage
rows.what: William Sneyd and Mary Blackbourne, whom the tree names as Samuel's parents
rows.got: Found, and it had been in the results list all along. Madeley All Saints, 27 March 1769, entry 68: William SNEYD, WEAVER, and Mary BLACKBOURNE, witnessed by Robert Sneyd and John Kidd. This archive reported the line unevidenced this morning without following it up.

rows.what: How and when the Wakefields reached Australia, and whether the passenger register gives Hannah's native place
rows.got: FOUND, with the register scan. The ship GENERAL HEWITT, Brisbane, 16 December 1854, 394 souls. James Wakefield 48, a MASON — matching the 1841 census's “Mason Journeyman” — with Hannah 48, Jabez 11, Zillah 8 and Ephraim 5; Hiram 16 a plumber and Aaron 14 entered separately among the single men, both native place BRISTOL; and Marion Wakefield 14, a domestic, among the single women, also Bristol. Marion is Miriam. The emigration is now dated to the day.

rows.src: QSA digital image DR38490 — the passenger register itself
rows.what: Whether the register gives Hannah Wakefield's own county
rows.got: It does not. Her county is a ditto mark under her husband's “Gloucester”, which is the household head's county and not a statement about her. The register plainly distinguishes the two — it enters her three eldest children as Bristol on the same day — so the ditto cannot be read as her birthplace. Hannah's origin remains the open question.

rows.src: FreeREG — every Saniger record in Gloucestershire, opened individually
rows.what: All 556 records read one by one and reconstituted into households, rather than searched by name
rows.got: 81 households assembled from 196 baptisms naming a father. Not one has a mother called Lydia; not one is a John and Lydia; there is a single Hannah baptised in the whole county, at Stinchcombe in 1730; and only three households bear children between 1795 and 1815. Hannah is not in Gloucestershire — which the 1841 census had already said by entering her as born out of the county.

rows.src: FreeBMD — deaths, Lydia Saniger and every spelling, 1841–1875
rows.what: Lyddya Sinegar of the 1841 census, who should have died in England
rows.got: Not there. A deliberately loose phonetic search — loose enough to return SCHONSWAR and SMOOKER — finds no Lydia Saniger, Sanigar or Sinegar death in Bristol in those thirty-four years. The nearest are an infant Lydia Ann Sanigear at Islington in 1847 and an unnamed SANIGAR at Thornbury in 1851. Either she died under a married surname, or under a spelling the index does not reach.

rows.what: Hannah Wakefield's exact birthplace, which 1841 does not give
rows.got: Not applicable, and worth recording as such: the family had emigrated. James Wakefield died at Brisbane in July 1857, so by 1861 there was nobody in England to enumerate. The plan to get Hannah's birthplace from a later English census was sound and the family had left before it could work. Reclassified 15 September 2026 from a null: the source does not cover the question, which is a different fact from the record not being there.

rows.src: FreeREG — the marriage of John Saniger and Lydia Jones
rows.what: About 1795–1804, wherever Hannah was born
rows.got: Cannot be attempted usefully. Hannah was born outside Gloucestershire and the archive does not know where, so there is no parish to search; and if the marriage was at Berkeley the transcript ends in 1677 regardless. This one needs Hannah's birthplace first, and that now depends on a certificate.

rows.src: FreeREG — Madeley All Saints, the two baptisms the tree asks for
rows.what: William Sneyd bapt. 1746 and Samuel Sneyd bapt. 1769, both said by the tree to be at Madeley
rows.got: Neither exists. Madeley holds Samuel 1745, Joseph 1746, John 1748, Simeon 1751 and no William; and its only Samuel is baptised 1781. The parish is transcribed continuously — 110 Sneyd records from 1699 — so both are real absences. This archive had been using a 1742 William instead, four years off the tree's date, and that child may be the one buried in 1744.

rows.src: Queensland historical BDM index — deaths, searched by MOTHER's name
rows.what: Every Queensland death registration whose mother is recorded as a Saniger
rows.got: THE ANSWER. Five of Hannah's children died in Queensland and every registration names her: Ephraim 1868 “Anna Sanniger”, Aaron 1896 “Hannah Sanegar”, Zillah 1900 “Hannah Saniger”, Hiram 1905 “Hannah Sanigar”, Miriam 1909 “Hannah Saniger”. Five clerks, forty-one years, four spellings — and the father given as James Wakefield on all five.

rows.src: Queensland historical BDM index — Hannah Wakefield's own death
rows.what: Her parents, from her own registration
rows.got: Registration 1873/C/603, died 4 July 1873 — matching the tree to the day. Her father is entered as “John JENNIGER”. The tree says John Saniger. A capital S read as a J is one of the commonest misreadings in nineteenth-century clerking, and the forename and the rest of the surname agree exactly. Her mother is not given.

rows.src: Queensland historical BDM index — James Wakefield's death
rows.what: The father of the family, died Brisbane 8 July 1857
rows.got: Registration 1857/B/135, and it names HIS father: RICHARD WAKEFIELD. A generation the archive did not have, and the first Wakefield above James anywhere.

rows.what: Miriam Wakefield's marriage, and her siblings'
rows.got: Miriam Wakefield married WILLIAM HARTLEY SNEYD on 15 November 1859 at Brisbane, registration 1859/B/255 — the marriage that joins the Wakefields to the Sneyds, and she was nineteen, not twenty-one as this archive had said. Her brothers Hiram and Aaron married Margaret and Elizabeth Ann BIRCH four months apart in 1861; Jabez married Margaret Fraser in 1863; Zillah married John Ludwig Frederick in 1871.

rows.src: Queensland historical BDM index — Lydia Saniger
rows.what: Whether Lyddya Sinegar of the 1841 census followed her family to Queensland
rows.got: No Lydia Saniger death is registered in Queensland under any spelling. She was seventy in 1841; the family did not emigrate until after 1849. She stayed, and died, in England.

rows.what: Any trace of Robert D'Arcy and Jean Ward at Portsea, where the tree says they married on 21 June 1779
rows.got: FOUND, and it is the first record of Robert D'Arcy in an English parish register this archive has ever had. Joseph D'ARCY, baptised Portsea St Mary 19 March 1780 — father ROBERT, mother JEAN. Nine months after the marriage the tree asserts, at the same church. It is the only D'Arcy record in the whole county.

rows.what: The real Sneyd line under the disproved Keele graft
rows.got: 110 Sneyd records at Madeley All Saints. The 1742 baptism that killed the Keele claim reads: William Sneyd, 12 September 1742, father William Sneyd. And two years later: “William, son of William SNEYD”, buried 29 September 1744. If that is the same child — and in one small parish it is the obvious reading — the archive's Sneyd line is anchored to a boy who died at two.

rows.what: The generation above Francis Murdoch of St Quivox
rows.got: 128 Murdoch records in Ayrshire, across Galston, Tarbolton, Ayr, Kirkoswald, Loudoun, Dailly, Beith and Dunlop — and St Quivox is not among the parishes with data. The county is thinly covered (202 Smiths for the whole of the eighteenth century) and the one parish this archive needs is not in it.

rows.what: Jean Ward, born South Leith 1754
rows.got: Midlothian's holding is Edinburgh, Canongate, Restalrig and Dalry. South Leith is not transcribed. Not a null result — the parish is simply not there.

rows.what: Richard Atkinson and Anne, and anything else in the county
rows.got: Zero records for the entire county. A control search for SMITH across the whole of the eighteenth century returns nothing at all. FreeREG lists County Limerick in its search form and holds no data for it.

rows.what: Surname Wakefield, whole county; then the household page itself
rows.got: THE FIND. HO107/374, enumeration district 13, page 10, dwelling 1615, Drivers Fields, civil parish of St Paul, Bristol: James Wakefield 35 a mason journeyman, Hannah 35, Hiram 4, Aaron 1, Miriam 1 — and Lyddya SINEGAR, 70, Independent. The tree records Hannah's mother as Lydia and her brother Jabez born at “Drivers Field”; neither was copied from this record, which nobody in the family had read.

rows.what: The same household ten years on, for the relationships and exact birthplaces 1841 does not give
rows.got: 221 Gloucestershire Wakefields are transcribed for 1851 and 31 of them in Bristol, but not this family. Nationally only 36% of the 1851 pieces are online and the piece covering Drivers Fields is not among them. A coverage gap, not an absence — and the record that would turn the Lyddya Sinegar inference into a fact.

rows.what: Whether the tree's “Berkley, Gloucester” is really Berkley in Somerset, which would explain Hannah being born out of county
rows.got: It is not. Berkley Somerset is transcribed in full — 7,967 records, 1545–1903 — and the family there is spelled SINGER in every one of 58 entries, with no Hannah baptised near 1805. A clean answer to a good question.

rows.what: Where the Vale of Berkeley Sanigers went
rows.got: 97 across Gloucestershire, 29 of them in Bristol, spelled SINEGAR, SUNIGAR, SENGEIR, SANGER and SINGER. The family did leave the Vale, and Bristol is where a good part of it went.

rows.what: Every register FreeREG holds for Bristol, checked before searching rather than after
rows.got: Four registers and 1,551 records for a city of 120,000: Countess of Huntingdon's Chapel (81, 1820–1837), Methodist Bishopston (98, 1891–1915), Moravian Maudlin Street (1,016, 1755–1865) and Temple of Holy Cross (356, 1834–1849). St Paul, Bristol — where the tree says Miriam Wakefield was baptised — is not among them. The Wakefield–Saniger join cannot be tested here, and any “not found” would have been a lie.

rows.src: FreeREG — coverage tool, the Vale of Berkeley
rows.what: Dursley, Cam, Thornbury, Stinchcombe, Coaley, Slimbridge, Uley, North Nibley, Wotton-under-Edge
rows.got: Dursley St James runs 1577–1951 with 30,784 records and Cam St George 1568–1939 with 17,150. Both cover the whole of the archive's Saniger chain. The /berkeley page had implied those generations were untestable because Berkeley stops in 1677; they were testable all along, three miles away.

rows.what: Fuzzy surname search, all record types, whole county
rows.got: 494 records. Cam 184, Dursley 156, Thornbury 55, Berkeley 18. Three baptisms match the tree's dates almost exactly: Thomas at Dursley 17 Mar 1711/12, William at Dursley 6 Nov 1743, William at Dursley 27 Sep 1770.

rows.src: FreeREG — the three Dursley baptisms, opened
rows.what: The full transcription of each, to read the fathers
rows.got: The chain fails. Thomas 1711/12 is the son of ABRAHAM; William 1743 the son of JOHN; William 1770 the son of SAMUEL. Three men who happen to be baptised in the right parish in the right years, and no two of them are father and son. The date-match was a coincidence.

rows.what: The generation the tree puts at 1805
rows.got: None. Not a coverage gap: Dursley runs to 1951 and Cam to 1939, so the window is well covered. The tree's 1805 Saniger does not exist in Gloucestershire.

rows.what: Where the family goes after the chain is supposed to leave Berkeley
rows.got: 139 records, continuous through the whole century, centred on Cam (67), Dursley (28) and Thornbury (17). The family never leaves the Vale — and in 139 records it never once marries a Wakefield.

rows.src: FreeREG — Hannah Saniger, GLS, SOM and WIL, 1780–1880
rows.what: The one Saniger the archive actually needs: Miriam Wakefield's mother
rows.got: 35 fuzzy matches and not one of them in Gloucestershire. All are Somerset and Wiltshire SINGER or SANGER — different families the phonetic match swept up. Hannah Saniger is not in the Gloucestershire registers.

rows.what: Miriam Wakefield, born Bristol 11 April 1840
rows.got: FOUND. Birth registered June quarter 1840, Bristol district, volume 11, page 183 — the only Miriam Wakefield registered anywhere in England between 1839 and 1843. A birth on 11 April falls in the June quarter exactly as it should. Her GRO certificate names her mother with her maiden surname, which would test “Saniger” directly.

rows.what: A Wakefield–Saniger marriage, every spelling, 1837–1870
rows.got: None. The earliest Saniger or Sanigar marriage registered in the Bristol district is John Sanigar in the March quarter of 1846 — six years after Miriam was born. Control-tested: the same harness returns 21,248 Wakefield marriages for 1838–1842, so the search works and the absence is real. James Wakefield and Hannah Saniger did not marry in Bristol after civil registration began on 1 July 1837.

rows.what: Every spelling of D'Arcy and Sneyd against Brisbane and Queensland papers, 1840–1950; obituaries, funeral notices, insolvency reports, memorial notices
rows.got: Lindesay D'Arcy's 1936 obituary, confirming five details of a eulogy delivered 74 years later and restoring one the family had lost — that he served in France. George Pitt D'Arcy's 1849 obituary and the verdict “gout which had flown to the head”. The 1926 insolvency and the 1927 fraudulent-preference action against the bank. Arthur Sneyd's memorial notices and “Ruby”. Vivian Claude Sneyd at Gallipoli.

rows.what: “Sneyd” and “D'Arcy” across every series; then item-level fetches through the JSON API
rows.got: Forty-one items under Sneyd. The find of the day: coronial file ITM2736504 (DR103140), an inquest nobody in the family knew existed. Also the 1873 insolvency of William Hartley Sneyd, Arthur's 1916 intestacy, four wills, two police staff files and nine land dealings.

rows.what: Every Sneyd, D'Arcy, Blum, Wakefield and Murdoch death registration, 1856–1996
rows.got: Sixty registrations, eighteen of them published. Queensland death registrations name the deceased's parents, which is why this one free index carries more proved relationships than every other source on this page combined.

rows.src: National Archives of Australia — RecordSearch, series B2455
rows.what: Three AIF service dossiers, read page by page at native resolution
rows.got: Arthur Hartley Sneyd 5050 (30 pp.), Vivian Claude Sneyd 1696 (21 pp.), Ernest Vivian William Sneyd 3891 (92 pp.). Arthur's corrected his trade from clerk to typist and his burial from “France” to no known grave.

rows.what: The Red Cross Wounded and Missing Enquiry Bureau file for 5050 Sneyd
rows.got: Twenty-three pages, six witness statements, six different answers. A friend still searching thirteen months later from a lecture room at New College, Oxford.

rows.what: Honours and awards recommendation files for Sneyd
rows.got: The Bar to Vivian Claude Sneyd's Military Medal, in full: Westhoek, 4 October 1917, signed by Lieut-Col A. Graham Butler and endorsed “Awarded”.

rows.what: D'Arcy wills in PROB 11; WO 97 discharge papers; ADM 101 surgeons' journals; Ordnance series
rows.got: PROB 11/1728/64 — Robert D'Arcy's own will, proved 4 July 1827, digitised and unordered. ADM 101/26/1, the surgeon's journal of the convict ship England, which names Major George Pitt D'Arcy four times and closes a 23-year loop on how he died.

rows.what: Full-text sweep of the colony's civil establishment lists for every family surname
rows.got: Thirty-seven years of Sneyds on the Queensland payroll. William Hartley Sneyd, Fount-room Overseer at the Government Printing Office on £225, in the public service from 1 February 1862 — matching his widow's sworn “about 12 years” to the year.

rows.what: Every spelling of Saniger, 1600–1677, plus a county-wide fuzzy sweep
rows.got: Forty-four Sainger entries at Berkeley and 238 across the county. One candidate baptism, 24 May 1655, giving a father the archive never had — Edward Sainger of Wanswell. And the unexpected result: the surname's centre is Dursley and Cam, not Berkeley.

rows.src: Connolly, Roll of Officers of the Corps of Royal Engineers
rows.what: Robert D'Arcy and Constantine D'Arcy
rows.got: Entry 203 — Robert's whole career, 2nd Lt 1776 to Major-General 1819, C.B., died Chatham 13 May 1827. Entry 335 — Constantine, died Chatham 6 May 1805. Neither entry records a parent, which is itself the finding.

rows.what: Murdoch of St Quivox, Ayrshire
rows.got: A generation documented. Also the reason the DNA points here: this is a quarter of the tested descendant and the archive has half its ancestor slots empty.

rows.what: One living descendant's result, against the tree's own prediction
rows.got: Agreement, not contradiction: British Isles 80.1% measured against 93.4% predicted. And the test that matters — cutting both grafts moves the prediction by 0.39 of a percentage point.

rows.src: National Archives of Australia — B2455, D'Arcy
rows.what: Lindesay Atkinson D'Arcy's AIF dossier, under every spelling of the name
rows.got: Nothing. The method was then control-tested by running the same query for his brother-in-law Arthur Sneyd, which returned his dossier at once — so the absence is real and not a bad search. The archive had previously claimed a fourteen-page dossier “is known to exist”; that claim was withdrawn.

rows.what: The will of the 4th Earl of Holderness
rows.got: No PCC will that can be found. This was the single best hope of testing whether the Earl acknowledged a natural son, and it is not there to test.

rows.what: An obituary or death notice for Major-General Robert D'Arcy, C.B. — RE-TESTED by reading the whole year
rows.got: Still empty, and now properly established. The first search recorded this; on 15 September 2026 all TWELVE monthly issues of 1827 and BOTH annual indexes were downloaded and read in full. Two D'Arcys appear in the entire year and neither is him: “Offord D'Arcy, Huntingdonshire”, a place name inside a marriage notice, and D'Arcy Wentworth of Sydney, a different man entirely. The only Chatham death reported that June is “Newham, esq. late of Basil-street”. Controls: the Deaths and Obituary sections are present in every issue, Chatham appears three times in June and Engineers five times in May. A Companion of the Bath and a colonel of Engineers died at Chatham and the magazine of record did not notice. That silence is load-bearing on /hornby and it has now been earned rather than assumed.

rows.what: A baptism for Robert D'Arcy, c.1750–1758
rows.got: Nothing, under any spelling. Combined with Connolly recording no parentage and the Gentleman's Magazine recording no death, the parentage question is not disputed — it is unknown.

rows.src: WO 149 — Royal Military Academy Woolwich cadet registers
rows.what: A cadet of the early 1770s
rows.got: The wrong record set entirely: WO 149 begins in 1790 and is held at Sandhurst. The archive had recommended it without checking its date range, and said so. Reclassified 15 September 2026 from a null: the source does not cover the question, which is a different fact from the record not being there.

rows.what: The citation for Vivian Claude Sneyd's first Military Medal
rows.got: The Gazette records the award but does not name him in a citation. The Bar was found instead, at the AWM.

rows.what: A service record for Samuel Charles Sneyd, Governor of Brisbane Gaol
rows.got: Searched twice. He appears exactly once in the whole QSA catalogue and it is not a service record. A man who ran a colonial gaol for over a decade has left no staff file that survives.

rows.what: Five generations of the Saniger chain, 1679 to 1805
rows.got: Not a null result and must not be reported as one: the Berkeley transcript stops in 1677. The records may well exist in the parish books; they are absent from the transcription, which is a different thing.

rows.what: Where Arthur Hartley Sneyd is commemorated
rows.got: Bot-blocked, twice. A free two-minute search that a person can run and this archive cannot.

rows.what: Mounted Police and convict-era records for Samuel Charles Sneyd
rows.got: The catalogue migrated to mhnsw.au and the old URLs are dead. Between houses.

rows.what: General searching beyond the two files reached by direct URL
rows.got: Mid-migration. Two documents were reached by constructing S3 URLs directly; the search itself would not answer.

rows.what: Newspaper coverage of William Hartley Sneyd's insolvency
rows.got: The QSA file proves the insolvency exists. Trove's search interface would not surface the notice, repeatedly. The file itself is not digitised.

rows.src: Smyth's Men and Armour for Gloucestershire, 1608
rows.what: The whole county, for the Saniger surname — all seventeen spellings this archive holds, plus every surname in Gloucestershire ending -gar, -gear, -ger, -gor and -gre
rows.got: Eleven men in four spellings — Saniger (5), Sanyger (3), Syniger (2), Sainger (1). One, John Sainger, weaver, is living in the hamlet of Saniger in Hinton parish, Berkeley. SANYGER and SYNIGER were not among the seventeen spellings held here.

rows.src: Smyth's Men and Armour for Gloucestershire, 1608
rows.what: Thirteen spellings of the surname that returned nothing: Sanigar, Sanigear, Sanegar, Saneger, Sannigar, Sanniger, Sannegar, Sanger, Sinegar, Sinnegar, Siniger, Sinigar, Sinager, Sineger
rows.got: All genuinely absent, control-tested: the same interface returned 676 men for Dursley and 42 for Halmore. Every form ending -GAR is missing from 1608, which dates the -GAR spellings as later than the -GER ones rather than older.

rows.src: Smyth's Men and Armour for Gloucestershire, 1608
rows.what: SWANHANGER, as both a surname and a place name
rows.got: Nothing under either. The tithing is written 'Saniger [in Hinton parish, Berkeley]' by 1608, so the older form had already gone out of written use — consistent with the deeds, which carry Swanhanger to 1741 only as an antiquarian spelling.

rows.what: The scanned text of the 1980 reprint (menarmourforglou0000smyt)
rows.got: A lending item: the full text returns HTTP 401 and the search-inside endpoints are retired. Reading it would need an Archive.org account and a loan. The 1902 edition's transcript at coaley.net answered instead.

rows.what: A register lookup: the marriage of John Saniger and Lydia at Berkeley St Mary the Virgin, c.1795–1800, and confirmation of Hannah Sanigor's baptism of 18 August 1804
rows.got: Answered in one day and declined: the office does not offer a research service of any kind. It named two routes instead — the Gloucestershire Family History Society, whose volunteers do lookups, and Ancestry, which holds the filmed county registers with marriages and banns to 1938. The record is not unreachable; this door is.

rows.src: Smyth, A Description of the Hundred of Berkeley (c.1639, printed 1885)
rows.what: The full text of volume 3 of The Berkeley Manuscripts, for Saniger, Sanyger, Swanhanger, Swonhungre and every OCR-plausible variant
rows.got: Fourteen occurrences of Saniger, three of Sanyger, eight of Swonhungre. Smyth heads the hamlet “Swonhunger; corruptly called Saniger”, describes it as thirteen dwelling houses in the manor of Hame, and gives its owner in 1639 with four generations of male ancestors — John, son of John, son of Maurice, son of Robert, son of William. Also Robert Saniger buying a manor in 1541 and John Saniger of Saniger acting as a trustee. Control: Berkeley 1,497 hits, Hinton 53, Nibley 73 in the same file.

rows.what: All spellings of the surname across every repository Discovery indexes: Saniger, Sanigar, Sanyger, Sainger, Syniger, Swanhanger, Swonhunger
rows.got: Seventy-one records under Saniger, forty-four under Sanigar, three under Swanhanger, two under Swonhunger, none under Syniger. Six that were new here — a fine of 1731 naming Maurice Saniger and Jane his wife, a consistory-court defamation of 1768, the 1617 trustee deed Smyth describes without dating, John Saniger yeoman in 1601, a coroner's inquest on Elizabeth Saniger aged 3 of Cam in 1856, and an inquisition post mortem of 1626 — plus twelve Berkeley Castle deeds naming people “of Saniger” between before 1291 and 1473. Sanyger and Sainger returned only Devon, Norfolk, Sussex and Reading records belonging to other families.

rows.what: All 26 Sneyd war dead, and the casualty record for Arthur Hartley Sneyd
rows.got: Casualty 1451888 confirms the Villers-Bretonneux MEMORIAL — not the military cemetery of the same name, which holds a different Sneyd, Rex, 49th Bn, died 14 June 1918. Service number 5050, 9th Bn A.I.F., died 20 August 1916 aged 22, son of Arthur and Martha Sneyd of James St., Wooloowin, born at Rockhampton. Nothing here was new; everything here was already published, and is now sourced to the authority instead of inferred.

rows.what: The baptism of LYDIA JONES at Wotton-under-Edge, about 1770, to William Jones and Sarah
rows.got: Not a null — the parish is not transcribed. Lydia Jones, Gloucestershire baptisms 1760–1785: nil. But JONES of any forename at WOTTON-UNDER-EDGE, all record types, 1740–1800: also nil — nought entries for the commonest surname in England across sixty years. The same search across the county returns 164 Jones baptisms in a narrower window, so the engine works and the county is covered. Wotton-under-Edge appears in FreeREG's place list and has effectively no eighteenth-century transcription behind it, which is the coverage-tool-versus-search disagreement this archive has already recorded once.

rows.src: Gloucestershire Registration Service Index (with the Gloucestershire FHS)
rows.what: All deaths registered under the stem SANIG across Gloucestershire, 1837–1899, sweeping in five-year steps
rows.got: Twenty-four deaths, each with the registrar's own register and entry number rather than a GRO quarterly reference — including LYDIA SANIGAR, 1851, register 3, entry 265, who this archive has wanted since it began. Coverage was checked before searching: Thornbury/Berkeley deaths complete 1837–1948, Dursley 1837–1937, Wotton-under-Edge 1837–1937. A free index nobody here had used.

rows.src: Staffordshire Name Indexes — Diocese of Lichfield and Coventry Wills, 1550–1810
rows.what: SNEYD, all 36 records, and SNEYD of MADELEY
rows.got: Thirty-six Sneyd wills, ten of them at Keele — and the tenth is RICHARD SNEYD, LABOURER, of Keele, 1772, in the same parish and the same court as four Ralph Sneyds, esquires and gentlemen. Sneyd of MADELEY returns nothing; control is the same search without a place, which returns all thirty-six.

rows.src: Staffordshire Name Indexes — the site as a whole
rows.what: The Madeley burials of the 1740s, and Lichfield bishop's transcripts generally
rows.got: Structurally out of scope. The site indexes twenty-six Staffordshire collections — wills, apprentices, asylums, gaol calendars, tithe awards, workhouse admissions — and no parish registers or bishop's transcripts of any kind. It cannot answer errand 19 and never could.

rows.src: Smyth, The Berkeley Manuscripts, volumes 1 and 3 (1883–85)
rows.what: Every occurrence of Swonhunger, Swanhunger, Saniger and Sanyger across both volumes — the twenty-five page references in Smyth's own index
rows.got: Forty-four distinct passages. A pedigree of the hamlet's owners from Thomas de Stone (died 1315–16) to John Swonhungre, who died without issue in 1401–2 leaving two sisters; the place in the free-warren charters of Henry II to Edward I; a grant of a yard land at Swonhunger dated 1189; Nigell of Swonhunger temp. Richard I; John de Swonhongre, esquire, in Lord Berkeley's retinue in 1326; and the hinge for the later branch — William Swonhunger, Crown lessee under Henry VIII, father of Robert, father of John.

rows.src: The National Archives — PROB 11 digitised wills
rows.what: Whether PROB 11/1825/326 (Elizabeth Saniger), PROB 11/1728/64 (Major-General Robert D'Arcy) and PROB 11/1991/312 can be downloaded
rows.got: All three are digitised and open, and all three read “£3.50 - sign in to get this free”. The charge is waived for any registered user and registration is free, so these are not paid records — they are free records behind a free account. This archive creates no accounts, so they stay on the errand queue, but at nil cost rather than £10.50.

rows.src: The National Archives — Discovery, the other surnames
rows.what: SINEGAR, SANIGRE, COTTON of Berkeley, WAKEFIELD with Saniger, and D'Arcy with the Royal Engineers at Chatham
rows.got: COTTON of Berkeley gives the first document from Catherine Cotton's side of the family: PROB 11/1056/294, the will of Benjamin Cotton, cordwainer of Berkeley, proved 16 September 1779, eleven months after her burial in the same parish. D'ARCY with Chatham returns Robert D'Arcy's own will and twenty plans of the Chatham Lines from 1804 to 1821 — MR 1/553/3, and the MFQ 1/1280 and MFQ 1/1315 series — drawn across the years this archive says he was chief engineer there.

rows.what: SINEGAR and SANIGRE as surnames
rows.got: Sanigre: nothing at all. Sinegar: three records and not one is a person — a Bisley police station called Sinegar House in 1950 and 1984, and an unrelated Sussex account of 1705. Both spellings are productive in the Bristol and Berkeley registers and neither has left a catalogued document anywhere.

rows.src: Gloucestershire Registration Service Index — births and marriages
rows.what: All births and all marriages under the stem SANIG, 1837–1893, swept in five-year steps
rows.got: Twenty-seven births and ten marriages, each with a local register and entry number, and the marriage index giving both partners — Ford, White, Stephens, Stockwell, Watts, Dore, Sinnett, Young, Powell. Read against the twenty-four deaths already taken, seven names appear as both a birth and a death at intervals of one to nine years. The birth form also accepts a MOTHER'S MAIDEN NAME as a search term, which makes a guessed maiden name testable.

rows.src: Whitworth Porter, History of the Corps of Royal Engineers (1889)
rows.what: Robert D'Arcy, and the Corps' own account of the stations and sieges he served at
rows.got: Five mentions, indexed by Porter as one man: Lieutenant Robert D'Arcy at the siege of Fort St Philip's, Minorca, 1781; “Robert D'Arcy, Barbados” in a station list, confirming from the Corps what this archive had inferred from two christenings; Lieutenant-Colonel R. D'Arcy as COMMANDING ENGINEER of the Copenhagen expedition of 1807; and as Commanding Royal Engineer at Walcheren in 1809, where — “an old man beyond sixty” — he refused to write a report for a wounded superior he claimed to outrank, was put under arrest, and apologised only after the court-martial was arranged. Free, out of copyright, and never opened here before.

rows.what: All SNEYD deaths in Staffordshire, 1837 onward — a free local index nobody here had used
rows.got: 276 Sneyd deaths, each with AN AGE AT DEATH, a sub-district and a local register reference — none of which the GRO quarterly index gives. Errand 10's target is there and independently confirms what this archive already had: SNEYD, Samuel, aged 77, 1855, HANLEY sub-district, registers at Stoke-on-Trent, reference HAN/011/023, matching the Hanley burial of 23 September 1855 aged 77 of 91 Well Street. The certificate can now be ordered against the local reference.

rows.what: Whether Bristol and Somerset have local registrars' indexes like Gloucestershire's and Staffordshire's
rows.got: They do not. The project lists Gloucestershire and Staffordshire — both used today, both productive — but neither Bristol nor Somerset has a dedicated local index. For the Bristol Wakefields and the Chew Magna Smiths there is no equivalent of the reference that found Lydia Sanigar.

rows.src: Internet Archive — Rudder, A New History of Gloucestershire (1779)
rows.what: Saniger, Swanhanger and the Berkeley hundred parishes in the full text
rows.got: The text download returns HTTP 503 and an error page. Control: the file contains nought occurrences of BERKELEY, DURSLEY and HINTON, which is impossible for this book — so the download failed rather than the book being silent. Recorded as unreachable, not as a null.

rows.src: Internet Archive — Collections for a History of Staffordshire (William Salt Society)
rows.what: Sneyd of Keele pedigrees, and any Madeley branch, in two volumes of the series
rows.got: Nothing genealogical in the two volumes reachable: one has no Sneyd at all, the other has exactly one — in the society's own list of subscribers, “Sneyd, Rev. Walter, Keele Hall, Newcastle”, a living member in the 1880s. The series runs to dozens of volumes and the pedigree material is in ones not identified here. Control: Staffordshire itself appears 90 and 49 times, so the files are sound.

rows.src: The National Archives — research guides and Discovery API
rows.what: Which series holds a Board of Ordnance engineer's commission of 1776; the piece-level arrangement of IR 26 for 1876; and the right series for a British death at Le Havre in 1843
rows.got: WO 54/240, Engineers 1755–1780, is the only Board of Ordnance commission book covering the 1770s, with WO 47/87–88 as the minutes that would date the appointment. IR 26 runs to 1903, not 1857, and the 1876 C–D will registers are IR 26/2941–2947, chosen by the folio number in IR 27/396/3. RG 35/8–13 is the France run for foreign death returns, gated by the digitised index RG 43/4. None of the three is name-indexed free.

rows.what: Whether the Death Duty registers stop in 1857, which would make the Catherine D'Arcy errand impossible
rows.got: They do not. 1857 is where the MICROFILMING stops — the registers themselves run 1796–1903 and the 1876 pieces are open, catalogued and held at Kew, merely unfilmed and offline. A widely repeated access boundary mistaken for a records boundary, and the errand survives it.

rows.src: Calendars of Inquisitions Post Mortem, volumes 5–8 (Edward II – Edward III)
rows.what: SWONHUNGER in every spelling, and THOMAS DE STONE, whose two daughters carry Smyth's pedigree
rows.got: Neither family is in four volumes of the printed Calendars. Controlled twice: Gloucester appears 230–334 times per volume and Berkeley 15–17, so the county is covered; and a fragment search on “hungr”/“hunge”, tolerant of the volumes' poor OCR, returns Gravenhunger, Clehungre and Trewonhan — names of exactly that shape — so the search reaches them. The explanation is structural: a royal inquisition was taken only for a tenant-in-chief, and the Swonhungers held of Lord Berkeley, not of the king. The absence is what the record type predicts.

rows.what: Swonhunger, Swanhunger, Swonhungre and Saniger across its published series
rows.got: A CAPTCHA on every search URL, in curl and in a real browser alike. This archive does not complete CAPTCHAs, so the site is unreachable from here. It publishes the Victoria County History and the calendars of Close, Fine and Patent Rolls, all of which would be worth a human's ten minutes.

rows.what: ROBERT D'ARCY in the establishment of the Corps of Engineers
rows.got: There by name, in the junior grade: “Practitioner Engineer and Second Lieutenant … Robert Beatson, ROBERT D'ARCY, Benjamin Slack, James Lees…”. It also corroborates Porter independently: all six engineers Porter names at the siege of Fort St Philip's in 1781 — Townshend, D'Arcy, Johnston, Douglas, Shipley, Fiddes — are in the 1778 establishment, in the ranks Porter gives them.

rows.what: Whether Robert D'Arcy appears before 1778, to settle Connolly's 1776 against the commission registers' 1778
rows.got: Not there — and it settles nothing. The control kills it: FIDDES, HOCKINGS, HUMFREY and SLACK, all printed beside him in 1778, return nought occurrences in both earlier volumes. Those lists do not carry the Practitioner Engineer grade at all, so the absence is the book's and not the man's. The two dates stand unreconciled and the document that would reconcile them is WO 54/240 at Kew.

rows.what: The seniority date behind Robert D'Arcy's first commission, to reconcile 1776 against 1778
rows.got: 17 JANUARY 1776, settled. The 1781 list interleaves each engineer with his date and D'Arcy's is a ditto inside a block headed “17 Jan. 76”, with the men after him breaking the ditto with their own later dates. The 1778 list carries the same run and Connolly's Roll agrees on the year. This archive had 1776 on five pages and 1778 on one; the outlier was the page that named a record series and claimed a superlative.

rows.what: Jane, Catherine and Charlotte D'Arcy in the 1861 census — and then whether FreeCEN's Sussex could have held them at all
rows.got: A null on 15 September, corrected the same day to an EMPTY, because the control was wrong. D'ARCY, ARCY, D ARCY and DARCEY return nothing; DARCY returns six people, all one Sussex-born household at Kemp Town, Brighton — Eliza b. Newhaven 1816, Daniel b. Bishopstone 1818, four children b. Brighton 1847–57. None can be a sister. THE FIRST CONTROL WAS SMITH, which returns the display cap of 1,000, and I read that as the county and the town being covered. It is not. The real control is a record known to be there: the three sisters ARE in the 1851 Sussex census under the surname ARCY, at HO107/1646 folio 357 page 59 schedule 172, 22 Western Cottages, Brighton — and FreeCEN returns NOUGHT for Arcy in Sussex in 1851. It does not hold that piece. A capped surname count measures volume, not coverage.

rows.what: Every D'Arcy in the army's own published record of its serving officers
rows.got: Three, and all three are this family. Entry 607, MAJOR-GENERAL ROBERT DARCY, C.B. — his whole service in one paragraph, eight ranks from 17 January 1776 to 12 August 1819, including a First Lieutenancy of 1784 and a Captaincy of 1793 this archive did not have. Entry 1667, LIEUT.-COL. JOSEPH D'ARCY — seven ranks from 1795 to 1816, and the Persian order given “for his conduct, while in the actual service of the King of Persia”. Entry 2098, MAJOR GEORGE D'ARCY — Ensign 39th Foot 1794 to Brevet Major 1813, “Served in the Peninsula, and has received a medal for the battle of Orthes”.

rows.what: Robert D'Arcy's parentage, birthplace or schooling — the oldest open question in this archive
rows.got: Not there, and the silence is worth something because of where it comes from. The Calendar prints schooling and origins when it has them: the very next entry, Major-General George Bridges, opens “After the usual course of instruction at Woolwich Academy”. For Robert D'Arcy it prints service and nothing else. The army's own book, compiled while he was alive and a Companion of the Bath, did not record where he came from.

rows.what: A death notice for Lieutenant-Colonel Joseph D'Arcy
rows.got: There, in the March issue at page 328, among the Hampshire deaths: “Feb. 7. At Homestead, Lymington, aged 68, Lieut.-Col. Joseph D'Arcy, late of the Royal Art. K.L.S.”, with his three commission dates and the Persian order “conferred for his conduct when in the actual service of the Shah of Persia”. A fourth independent notice of a death this archive already held from three newspapers — and the one that breaks the tie on his age, since two of the four now agree he was 68. The contrast with his father is the point: the same magazine, twenty-one years earlier, said nothing at all about a major-general.

rows.src: The National Archives — Discovery, series RG 37
rows.what: What RG 37/65/2 actually is, the reference this archive cites for the three sisters' burials at Hove
rows.got: Not a parish register. RG 37 is “General Register Office: Removal of Graves and Tombstones”, 1923–2007, described by TNA as “copies of records of local authorities and the Church Commissioners relating to burial ground removals”. RG 37/65/2 is “Hove: St Andrew's Old Church: Part 2. BURIAL GROUND SECTION A”, c.1975, one of twenty-three parts lettered A to X. The three dates stand; the page's description of the document did not, and is corrected. The gain is the section letter: three sisters in one section is a family plot.

rows.src: Gloucestershire Registration Service Index — coverage for Bristol
rows.what: Whether the free county index that found Lydia Sanigar could also reach the Bristol Wakefields — errand 12, Miriam Wakefield 1840
rows.got: It cannot. The index's districts are Cheltenham, Cirencester, Forest of Dean, Gloucester, North Cotswolds, Stroud and Warwick South, with Berkeley, Dursley, Uley and Wotton-under-Edge beneath them. Bristol is a registration county of its own and is not in it — which matches the UKBMD finding that Bristol has no local index at all. The Berkeley Sanigers are reachable this way and the Bristol Wakefields are not.

rows.what: The sisters in the two censuses either side of 1861, and a coverage test against a household known to exist
rows.got: Neither year holds them, and neither year can be trusted to. 1871: D'ARCY returns one man, John D'Arcy born Liverpool 1847 at Withyham; ARCY and DARCY nothing. 1851: DARCY returns one woman, Mary Darcy born Essex 1798 at Ore; ARCY nothing at all — although this archive has the three sisters in the 1851 Sussex census under precisely that surname, at 22 Western Cottages, Brighton. So FreeCEN's Sussex is partial in a way its result counts conceal: Smith hits the 1,000 cap in 1851, 1861 and 1871 alike, while a piece containing a known household is simply absent.

rows.what: All SNEYD births and marriages in Staffordshire from 1837, a free local index never used here
rows.got: 391 births and 322 marriages. The births carry the MOTHER'S MAIDEN NAME and the marriages name both partners AND THE CHURCH, neither of which the GRO index gives. It names a woman this archive knew only as “Ann”: JAMES SNEYD married ANN BIDDULPH in 1842 at STOKE, ST PETER, reference 31/03/214. Four Sneyd births carry Biddulph as the mother — Elizabeth Ann 1839 Shelton, Mary Julia 1842 Hanley, Catherine 1845 Hanley, James Arthur 1850 Hanley — and three match the Well Street household exactly, supplying full forenames for the “Mary J” and “James A” the censuses gave as initials. Catherine is new here.

rows.src: Staffordshire BMD — the archive's own Sneyd marriages
rows.what: Whether the index could reach this family's own marriages
rows.got: Mostly not, and for a structural reason worth stating. The index begins in 1837. Samuel Sneyd married Elizabeth Margaret Oliver at AUDLEM, CHESHIRE in 1809 — wrong county and twenty-eight years too early. His son Samuel Charles married at Camden, NEW SOUTH WALES in February 1837, the very year the index opens, and every later Sneyd marriage this archive holds is in Queensland. The parents stayed and the sons emigrated, so the only marriage the index can reach is the one that stayed: James the engraver, at Stoke in 1842.

rows.what: Swonhungre, Swonhongre, Swonhunger, Swonhangre, Swanhanger, Swanhunger — the forms the clerks actually used, as opposed to the modern Saniger searched on 14 September
rows.got: 195 unique records across thirteen spellings — 178 at Berkeley Castle, 5 at Gloucestershire Archives, 5 at Kew, 3 at Birmingham, and one each at Bristol, Hertford and the National Library of Wales. SWONHUNGRE alone returns 126 against 71 for Saniger. Seventeen of the twenty-five read closely were new to this archive, including three carrying genealogical statements.

rows.src: TNA Discovery — spellings that return nothing
rows.what: Sanigre, Sannigar, Synigar, Swonhanger, Swanhangar — control on the alias list itself
rows.got: Nought for all five, against the same catalogue that returns 126 for Swonhungre in the same query shape. The control that could have failed did not: the search works, these forms simply were not used. Five of this site's alias spellings are therefore modern conjecture rather than attested variants.

rows.what: Whether the muniments Jeayes calendared in 1892 are catalogued in more detail now
rows.got: They are, item by item, and free to search without an account. 178 records under the medieval spellings, each with a calendar description naming parties, land, rent and witnesses, and each quoting the GC number to cite when requesting the document at Berkeley. Errand 51 asked for exactly this and can be closed.

rows.what: ROBERT and JOSEPH D'ARCY, both spellings, 1770–1830 — free, full-text, no account
rows.got: Neither man appears. All twenty-two notices naming a Darcy or D'Arcy between 1770 and 1789 are other people — Darcy Tancred, Darcy Burnell of Winkburn, Darcy Molineux, Sir Robert Darcy Hildyard, Darcy Linton, John Pomeroy Darcy, Arthur Darcy, and Darcy Lever, which is a place in Lancashire. Controlled first: the decade holds 1,057 notices mentioning «Lieutenant» and 245 mentioning «Ordnance», so the corpus is present and searchable.

rows.src: The London Gazette — why the null is structural
rows.what: Whether the Ordnance gazetted Corps of Engineers commissions at all in 1776
rows.got: It did not yet. Notices mentioning «Corps of Engineers»: 1774 none, 1775 none, 1776 three — one for the Chief Engineer in Ireland and two reprints of a Bengal notice. The practice appears during the American war (Shewbridge, May 1778) and is routine by the mid-1780s (promotions 1783; «Office of Ordnance… James Glenie», February 1787). Robert D'Arcy's commission of 17 January 1776 predates the Ordnance's habit of publishing, which is why the Army List seniority column and not the Gazette is what settles the date.

rows.src: The London Gazette — what it did give
rows.what: When the Corps of Engineers became the ROYAL Engineers
rows.got: Issue 12850, page 197, 23 April 1787: «His Majesty, by Warrant of this Day's Date, has been pleased to direct, that the Corps of Engineers shall in future take the Name of the Corps of Royal Engineers, and be so stiled and called.» Robert D'Arcy was commissioned into the Corps of Engineers in 1776 and the corps was renamed under him, eleven years in.

rows.what: Whether Gloucestershire's returns survive — the oath taken by nearly every adult male, parish by parish
rows.got: They do not. The surviving returns are a single alphabetical series of county bundles at the Parliamentary Archives, listed in Discovery as YHL/PO/JO/10/1/77 to /109: Berkshire, Buckinghamshire, Cambridgeshire, Cheshire, Cornwall, Cumberland, Denbighshire, Devon, Dorset, Durham, «Essex, Hampshire, Hertfordshire, Huntingdonshire», Kent, Lancashire, Lincolnshire, Middlesex, Northumberland, Nottinghamshire, Oxfordshire, Shropshire, Somerset, Staffordshire, Surrey, Sussex, Warwickshire, Westmorland, Wiltshire, Worcestershire and Yorkshire. GLOUCESTERSHIRE IS ABSENT FROM A RUN THAT GOES STRAIGHT THROUGH WHERE IT BELONGS — the piece that would hold it holds Essex and Hampshire instead. The alphabet is the control, and it could have failed.

rows.src: The Protestation Returns — what DOES survive
rows.what: Staffordshire, for the Sneyds
rows.got: YHL/PO/JO/10/1/105, «Staffordshire, Surrey». The returns survive for the Sneyd county and not for the Saniger one. Of no immediate use — this archive's Sneyds are documented from 1809, a hundred and seventy years later — but recorded so the next reader does not re-test it.

rows.src: E 179 and Gloucestershire Archives — the hearth tax
rows.what: Whether a 1671–72 Gloucestershire hearth tax survives, and whether it is readable from here
rows.got: It survives twice over and neither copy is online. Gloucestershire Archives D383/1, «Negative photostat of Gloucs. Hearth Tax enrolment + part transcript», 1671–1672. At Kew, E 179/329, 1670–1674, a bundle of 400 folios that «includes names of individuals» — about four hundred paper exemption certificates. Both are errands, not reads.

rows.what: A single bundle transcribing the three sources this archive most wants
rows.got: «Transcriptions of entries in MEN AND ARMOUR, 1608; in HEARTH TAX RETURNS, 1664, 1672; POLL TAX RETURNS, 1678.» One reference covering the muster this archive has already read, the hearth tax it wants, and a poll tax it did not know existed — all transcribed, all in one place, and all in Gloucester.

rows.what: Whether it reaches Berkeley hundred, where the Swonhungres were
rows.got: It does not. Gloucestershire Archives D 1874/1 photostats the surviving originals and lists every membrane: Salmonsbury, Holford and Greston, Kiftsgate, Tibblestone, Rapsgate, Bradley, Crowthorne, Brightwells Barrow, Longtree, Cirencester, Bisley, and St Briavels. BERKELEY HUNDRED IS NOT AMONG THEM. The surviving membranes are Cotswold and Forest; the Vale is lost. A named list of what survives is a better null than a search that returns nothing.

rows.what: ROBERT D'ARCY read year by year instead of at three points — free full text on the Internet Archive
rows.got: Four editions, four positions. 1783: SECOND LIEUTENANT of the Corps of Engineers, seven years after commissioning, in an intact ditto-chain — «John Humfrey 17 Jan. 1776 · James Fiddes do. · Richard Hockings do. · Robert Beatfon do. · Robert D'Arcey do. · Benjamin Slack 4 Mar.» 1802: CAPTAIN, Corps of Royal Engineers, p.409. 1803: Captain of the corps at p.288 and MAJOR in the army's own list at p.36. 1821: «D'Arcy, Lt. Col. Joseph, Royal Art.» A third printed confirmation of 17 January 1776, after the lists of 1778 and 1781.

rows.src: The Army List of 1783 — a spelling, not a silence
rows.what: Why outside catalogues do not return him
rows.got: The 1783 compositor sets the name ROBERT D'ARCEY, with an E. This site's own alias list has folded «d'arcey» and «darcey» into the D'Arcy group for weeks; the searches run against the London Gazette and the Internet Archive had not used it. The same fault as the Swonhungre sweep on the same day: a good alias list, never spent on somebody else's index.

rows.src: Whitworth Porter, History of the Corps of Royal Engineers, VOLUME 2
rows.what: Robert D'Arcy and Joseph D'Arcy, full text, free
rows.got: Neither appears in 1.5 million characters. Controlled by subject rather than by name: the volume mentions the Peninsula 48 times, Waterloo 11 and THE CRIMEA 43. It is the post-1815 volume, and Robert D'Arcy's service ran 1776 to about 1809 — volume 1's territory, which this archive has already read. Joseph was Royal Artillery, not Engineers, so no volume of Porter is the right book for him.

rows.src: John Smyth, Description of the Hundred of Berkeley (Berkeley MSS vol. 3)
rows.what: Re-read for the hamlet rather than for the pedigree
rows.got: Forty-nine mentions of Swonhunger. Three more alias statements beyond the famous one — «Swonhunger ats Saniger» in the formal list of the hamlets of Hamfallow, and «Sanyger ats Swonhunger» in a fine of Henry VII's reign. «Ats» is alias, not corruption. And a named freehold, OLDMINSTER, with its own tithe barn, which reappears as «Messuage called Oldminsters in Swanhanger [Saniger in Hinton]» in Gloucestershire Archives D654/III/9 of 1690–1741.

rows.src: FreeREG, at PARISH level — the control first
rows.what: SMITH in Berkeley, Gloucestershire, all years — to find what FreeREG's Berkeley transcript actually covers before reading any absence
rows.got: 3 exact and 36 uncertain results, and every one of them falls between 1653 and 1677 — Berkeley St Mary, «Other Transcript». So FreeREG's Berkeley holding is a SEVENTEENTH-CENTURY FRAGMENT of about thirty years, not a parish register run. The control could have failed — a common surname over two centuries of Berkeley would have returned hundreds — and instead it drew the window.

rows.what: SANIGER, against that measured window
rows.got: 0 exact results. The 38 «uncertain» are records whose characters are illegible in the transcript, the same set the Smith control returned. The null is real but NARROW: it covers about 1653–1680 and nothing else. This archive's Sanigers at Berkeley are documented in 1601 and then from 1692, so the gap FreeREG could speak to is thirty years wide and it is silent across them.

rows.what: Whether Awre and Blakeney — the Forest parishes — are covered at all
rows.got: They are not. FreeREG has data for 189 Gloucestershire places and the list includes Berkeley, Dursley, North Nibley, Slimbridge, Thornbury, Uley and Woodmancote — but neither Awre nor Blakeney. Any Awre search would have returned nothing for a reason that has nothing to do with the family.

rows.what: SANIGER and its variants across the whole county catalogue
rows.got: 127 unique records across six spellings, 33 of them at Gloucestershire Archives, spread from 1601 to the 1990s. Seven were new, and the shape of them is the finding: D2957/41/38, /39, /47, /48, /179, /187 and /190 are Berkeley estate deeds in which SANIGER IS THE LAND, not the party — Abevan, Hathway, Morse, Smith, Plomer and Vizard holding «at Saniger». One may be a person: D2078/BOX 23/4 of 1649, «Huntley, Saniger & Smyth». The catalogue confirms what Bigland and Smyth both say — a hamlet that far more people lived in than were named for.

rows.src: The Manorial Documents Register and Gloucestershire Archives
rows.what: Court rolls for AWRE, the Forest parish this archive cannot otherwise reach
rows.got: They survive in an almost unbroken run, and nobody here had looked. D2156/1 is a surrender of 1387, 10 Richard II; D2156/2 of 1439; D2156/3 of 1573; D2156/4 of 1577/8. D421/M7 holds the court rolls 1588–91 and the Hundred of Bledisloe for 1591. D3270/362 runs 1671, 1688–93, 1695–1745, 1747–66, 1768–1835, 1837–46, 1848–75, 1877, 1880–1. D3270/363 covers Awre and Etloe 1760–1886. Court rolls name tenants generation on generation, and this run spans the whole gap between the muster of 1608 and John Saniger's marriage about 1797.

rows.src: The Manorial Documents Register — the other two manors
rows.what: Hamfallow and Hinton, where the Berkeley-side Sanigers held
rows.got: Nothing separate survives. Hamfallow returns five hits and four are nineteenth-century gamekeeper registers; «manor of Hinton» Berkeley returns nought. Both were parts of the manor of Ham within the Berkeley estate rather than manors in their own right — which is why their records are inside the Berkeley Castle Muniments and not in a separate manorial series, and it is the same structural reason the Swonhungers generate no royal inquisition.

rows.src: Samuel Rudder, A New History of Gloucestershire (1779)
rows.what: SANIGER and SWONHUNGER, full text, free — 5.7 million characters
rows.got: Not there, under any spelling, and the null is informative because the control holds: Rudder mentions Berkeley 804 times and his index carries «Wanfwell in Berkeley 280», Hamfallow, Halmore and Alkington. At page 280 he enumerates the tithing — «6. Hamfallow, in which are Wanſwell, Wanniſwell, or Wanſel; part of Halmore; and Hamfallow» — and SANIGER IS NOT IN IT. Smyth listed it under Hamfallow in 1639 and Bigland under Hinton in 1791. Rudder, between them, lists it nowhere.

rows.src: Rudder, 1779 — what the same paragraph did give
rows.what: The Thorps, who inherited the Swonhunger estate
rows.got: «Thorp of Wanſwell held his lands to guard a tower in Berkeley-caſtle, called THORP'S-TOWER, which was built in the reign of king Edward the Third. Thomas Thorp died ſeized of the manor of Wanſwell, 17 H. 8. Thomas his ſon had livery thereof 29 H. 8.» Smyth's pedigree ends in 1401 with the estate passing through Isabel Swonhunger to John Thorpe of Bristol; Rudder carries that family to 1525 and says how they held — by castle-guard, at a named tower.

rows.what: SANIGER and every variant, across the digitised volumes
rows.got: One hit, and it corrects this archive. The serial reviewed Maclean's 1902 edition of Smyth's MEN AND ARMOUR FOR GLOUCESTERSHIRE — the very muster /saniger-1608 is built from — and listed its misreadings: «Thus SAINGER SHOULD READ SANIGER.» So the eleventh man, the one living in the hamlet the surname came from, is JOHN SANIGER OF SANIGER, and the muster holds three spellings in 1608, not four. Now correction 31.

rows.src: Gloucestershire Notes and Queries — the rest of the run
rows.what: Whether the serial carries anything else on this family
rows.got: Three further volumes read in full text — 2.5, 1.8 and 1.7 million characters — and not one mention of any spelling of the name. Controlled: the same volumes mention Berkeley 234, 91 and 51 times, so the parish is well within the serial's range. The family was too small for an antiquarian serial to notice, which is consistent with Rudder omitting the hamlet altogether in 1779.

rows.what: CHARLOTTE DARCY, died Brighton 1869, whose GRO reference this archive already holds
rows.got: «Darcy Charlotte 73 Brighton 2b 152» — age, district, volume and page, matching what /sussex-sisters already published. A control that could have failed and did not, and it was needed: FreeBMD SILENTLY REFUSES a date range of more than a few years, redisplaying its own search form, which is indistinguishable from an empty result. Three searches were recorded as nought before the control showed they had never run.

rows.what: SANIGAR deaths, 1850–1852, against a range narrow enough to execute
rows.got: All three. JOHN SANIGAR, March quarter 1850, Thornbury, vol 11 page 401. LYDIA SANIGAR, September quarter 1851, Thornbury, vol 11 page 329. MARY ANN SANIGAR, December quarter 1851, Thornbury, vol 11 page 369. Each quarter is marked by FreeBMD as more than 99 per cent transcribed. This archive already had all three from the Gloucestershire Registration Service's LOCAL register — 3/146, 3/265, 3/282 — so two independent indexes now agree, and Lydia's certificate can be ordered from the GRO as well as from Gloucester.

rows.src: Berkeley Castle Muniments — all 200 records, not the 25 read first
rows.what: Every catalogue description under every spelling, read for relationship language
rows.got: Twenty-five phrases tie the surname to a relationship and six were new: John son of Thomas (1311); Thomas son of John (early 14th cent.); THOMAS SON OF WILLIAM, MAUD HIS WIFE AND JOHN THE YOUNGER THEIR SON in one Hinton lease (mid 14th cent.); John son of John and Alice his wife (15th cent.); John Swonhongre and Edith his wife (1377); and the wardship of 1390. The other 175 are largely witness lists — Thomas de Swonhungre witnesses Berkeley charters from the mid-13th century to about 1311 beside the same circle of Berkeley officials.

rows.what: Whether the tenure this archive inferred can be documented
rows.got: It can, in the lord's own words: «Thomas has granted to John the marriage of John Swonhongre, son and heir of Elias Swonhongre, WHICH CAME TO THOMAS BECAUSE ELIAS HELD OF THOMAS BY KNIGHT SERVICE.» The archive had reasoned from silence that the Swonhungers generate no royal inquisition because they were mesne tenants of Berkeley. The reasoning was right and can now be retired in favour of the deed. It also confirms Smyth's statement that this John was «in ward to Thomas lord Berkeley», and shows why.

rows.src: The Berkeley deeds, read for topography rather than people
rows.what: How the hamlet was approached, and whether any field name survives
rows.got: Five deeds map the approach without a map: the king's highway from Longebrugge to Swonhunger (mid 13th cent.); Alagrene street in the west part of Berkeley towards Swonhungre (1287); the field called Stodfold near Swonhungre (1317); the path from Berkel' to Swonhungre through LE WESTFELD in the furlong of Kyngakre (1322); and le Muleweye, the road from Berckel' to Swonhungre at Lokedonne (1324). LE WESTFELD is the same field named in D2957/41/18 of 1601 — «3 acres of arrable in WESTFIELD, SANIGER, Berkeley» — 279 years later. A continuity of place, not of blood.

rows.what: What the series is, after three hits came out of one shelfmark
rows.got: «MS 3549 · 1200–1704 · SMYTH, JOHN (1567–1641), ANTIQUARY — MISCELLANEOUS DEEDS AND MANORIAL RECORDS COLLECTED BY JOHN SMYTH.» It is the steward's own working collection, gathered while writing the books this archive has spent a week testing. It explains the duplicate: the 1377 grant is BCM/A/1/24/185 at Berkeley Castle and MS 3549/20 here because Smyth kept a copy.

rows.src: MS 3549 — the court rolls inside it
rows.what: Whether Smyth's collection reaches the manors this family held in
rows.got: It does, on both sides of the gap. MS 3549/89 is the court roll of the MANOR OF HAM AND HYNTON, Courts Baron of 12 September 1587 to 15 March 1587/8 — the manor containing Hamfallow, and the tithing Bigland places Saniger in, fourteen years before this archive's earliest Saniger deed. MS 3549/182 is a copy court roll of ALKINGTON, 1624, where Edward Sanniger held in 1694. Twenty-two court rolls in the series in total. Neither is digitised, and both are at Birmingham, not Gloucester.

rows.src: Hertfordshire Archives, DE/M/95 — read in full
rows.what: Why a Gloucestershire deed sits in a Hertfordshire collection, and what the deed actually says
rows.got: DE/M is «Personal and family papers of the CAPELLS, EARLS OF ESSEX… title deeds of their Essex and Hertfordshire» estates, and John Capel is the first party — so the deed left Gloucestershire in his family's muniments. The full description is far richer than the search snippet: a purparty of «THE INHERITANCE IN HAMME OF JOHN DE WYKE» divided between JOAN CAPEL, ALICE DE SWONHONGRE and AGNES DE LOREWYNGE, each named as the ancestor through whom her heir holds. Alice was one of three coheirs of John de Wyke — the land came into this family through a woman. Wyke is the hamlet next to Swonhunger in Smyth's list.

rows.src: Edward Sanniger, mariner of Chepstow — the two references
rows.what: Whether his will can be read from here
rows.got: Both references confirmed and described. IR 26/352/152 at Kew is the ESTATE DUTY ABSTRACT — «Abstract of Will of Edward Sanniger, Mariner of Chepstow, Monmouthshire. Proved in the Llandaff», 28 November 1806. LL/1806/24 at the National Library of Wales is the will itself, «Diocese: Llandaf, Parish: Chepstow». Neither catalogue entry names a relative, so nothing yet connects him to this family — Chepstow is across the Severn from the Saniger fisheries and that is the whole of the case so far.

rows.src: National Library of Wales probate images
rows.what: Reading LL/1806/24 directly
rows.got: archives.library.wales serves a bot check — «Performing security verification… protect against malicious bots». This archive does not complete bot checks, so the will stays unread rather than being recorded as absent. The catalogue reference is firm and the document is digitised; only the route is closed.

rows.src: Thomas Sanniger, Able Seaman of HMS Eurydice
rows.what: The seaman's will of 1794, ADM 48/84/222
rows.got: Confirmed and no more: «Will of Sanniger, Thomas. Rank/Rating: Able Seaman. Ship Name: Eurydice. Ship's Pay Book number: 193», 24 February 1794. The catalogue gives rank, ship and pay-book number and no kin. Seamen's wills name next of kin in the document, which is the reason to order it — and the reason a catalogue search cannot settle whether he belongs here.

rows.src: Transactions of the Bristol and Gloucestershire Archaeological Society
rows.what: All 67 digitised volumes, every spelling, with each volume's Berkeley mention count as its own control
rows.got: Five volumes carry the name and two are substantial. VOLUME 22 (1899) prints Berkeley-area deeds in FULL ENGLISH TRANSLATION rather than calendar summary, including the indenture of 1 May 1329 and the partition of 22 July 1353. VOLUME 10 prints a Daubeney pedigree carrying the Swonhungers as a branch, sourced to two royal inquisitions and to Smyth. Volume 21 has «Katherine, daughter of John Harris of Sanigar»; volumes 45 and 46 list W. Sanigar of Barton Hill, Bristol, as a member in 1923.

rows.src: TBGAS volume 22 — the 1329 indenture in full
rows.what: Who Alice was, and where Wanswell came from
rows.got: «ELYANORA DE STONE, MOTHER OF THE AFORESAID ALICE AND JOAN» — so Alice, wife of John son of John de Swonhungre, and Joan, wife of John le Serjeant, are SISTERS and coheirs of Thomas de Stone, and their mother is named for the first time anywhere this archive has read. The Serjeants released to the Swonhungres everything in WANSWELL «of the heritage of the aforesaid Thomas de Stone», which is why a man is «Thomas Swonhungre of Wanswell» in 1356. Smyth said Alice was «younger daughter and coheir of Thomas de Stone»; the deed confirms him and adds her mother.

rows.what: Smyth's «third partition of the family lands in 27 Edward III»
rows.got: Printed entire: «William brother and heir of Thomas de Swonhunger» and John Serjeant the younger divide all they hold in common in Ham, Cam, Stinchcombe, Kingscote and Haselcote, «EXCEPT THE FISHERY IN SEVERN WHICH IS EXCEPTED FROM THIS PARTITION, AND WILL REMAIN IN CO[MMON]». The archive had Smyth's one-line description; this is the document, and it keeps the Severn fishery undivided — the same fishery Jeayes's charters reserve on Wednesdays and Fridays.

rows.what: Whether the last generations can be dated from record rather than from Smyth
rows.got: They can. Isabel Daubeney (ob. before 1393) married Elias Swonhonger; Elias died 13 Richard II (1389/90), having married Jone daughter of John Bill; JOHN SWONHONGER WAS AGED 18 IN 1393 and died 3 Henry IV (1401/2) without issue; Isabel Swonhonger married John Thorp. Sourced to the inquisition post mortem of John Wauton (16 Ric. II pt 1 no. 16), the inquisition «melius scire» on the heirs of Elizabeth Wauton (18 Ric. II no. 81), and Smyth p.370. An age of 18 in 1393 fits the sale of his marriage in December 1390 exactly. And Smyth's «John de Albiniaco alias Albeny» is DAUBENEY.

rows.src: TBGAS volume 10 — and a correction to this archive's own reasoning
rows.what: Whether «no royal inquisition» is true without qualification
rows.got: It is not. In 1394 a royal commission, by writ of 21 November 18 Richard II, went to the escheator of Gloucestershire to enquire whether JOHN SWONHONGRE and others «had become the heirs general of John and Cecilia Daubeney», whose Kingsholme and Hinton Daubeney lands had fallen in. The Swonhungers hold of Berkeley by knight service and so generate no Crown inquisition FOR THE BERKELEY LAND — now documented by BCM/A/4/2/22 — but through the Daubeney marriage they are named in royal inquisitions after all. The claim was right about Berkeley and too broad about everything else.

rows.src: J. H. Cooke, «Wanswell Court, and its Occupants for seven centuries», TBGAS vol. VI (1881–82)
rows.what: Whether anybody had already joined the medieval Swanhungers to the later Sanigers
rows.got: Somebody had, a hundred and forty years ago: «They were an old Berkeley family, whose patrimonial house and estate in the neighbourhood is still called SANIGER FARM, AND WAS SOLD BY EDWARD SANIGER TO THE EARL OF BERKELEY IN 1774.» The article also gives the descent from Thomas de Stone (d. 1316) through his younger daughter ALICE, who «married John Swanhunger, or Saniger», to the John who died without issue in 1402 and his sister Isabel who married John Thorpe, burgess of Bristol. Graded INFERRED: it is a careful scholar's conclusion in a footnoted article, not a chain of deeds set out, and this archive's rule is that a conclusion is evidence of reasoning rather than of fact.

rows.what: Whether the castle-guard story Rudder repeats has a document behind it
rows.got: It has one, and Cooke refused to accept it without: «The only documentary evidence of this Castle-guard tenure which I have met with is in a COURT ROLL FOR THE MANOR OF HAM, holden on the 26th May, 42 Eliz. (A.D. 1600), when the Homage presented the death of NICHOLAS THORPE, who died seised of the manor of Wanswell, holden by the sixteenth part of a knight's fee, the yearly rent of £4 8s. 8d., and by keeping one tower in the Castle of Berkeley called Thorpe's Tower.» The chief rent «was regularly paid until 1818, when it was extinguished by Earl Fitzhardinge's purchase of the estate».

rows.src: My own sweep of TBGAS volume 6, first attempt
rows.what: A control failure caught by the broader sweep
rows.got: Volume 6 was probed by hand earlier the same day for «Swonhung» and «Swonhong» and returned NOUGHT — so it was nearly set aside. Cooke's article spells the name SWANHUNGER and SANIGER throughout, neither of which those two patterns can match. The wider sweep, which carried ten spellings, found it immediately. The same fault as the D'Arcey one: a good alias list, not spent on the search actually being run.

rows.what: Whether a fine naming this family can be found without going to Kew
rows.got: It cannot. CP 25/1 survives at Kew but is catalogued ONLY AT PIECE LEVEL — «GLOUCESTERSHIRE: Feet of fines for 14-24 Hen VII: 38-77 membranes» is a typical entry, naming a county and a span of regnal years and not one party. No free, name-indexed published abstract exists for the county: searches for «feet of fines» and «pedes finium» with Gloucestershire return nothing on the Internet Archive, and Discovery returns only the piece descriptions. A fine naming a Swonhungre is therefore unfindable by search and would require reading membranes.

rows.what: Where the Wanswell estate came from, before Alice carried it in
rows.got: Four generations and two women. «THOMAS DE STONE, SON AND HEIR OF ROBERT SON OF ROBERT DE STONE» surrenders a holding he cannot pay £11 a year for, «on the advice of Master William de Kyngescote, Robert de Bradeston, JULIANA HIS MOTHER, Robert Wyther and his other friends», and takes instead a smaller one at £4 10s — a villein virgate «with Hugh and his issue and chattels», half-virgates, «a field called WYNTMELLEFELD with an enclosed pasture called OLDEFISCHWERE», 2 acres at Stone and 4 at Woodford. That smaller holding IS Wanswell. Cooke, in 1882, says of this deed that it «seems to be the only foundation of the tenure of any part of the Wanswell estate from Berkeley Castle» — he was reading it, and this archive now has its reference.

rows.what: The Wauton and Daubeney chain behind the Swonhunger inheritance
rows.got: «Andrew Wauton, husband of Elizabeth Gifford, reversioner after ELIAS DAUBENAY», 28 June 1383. It confirms the chain the TBGAS pedigree sets out, and supplies a small suggestive detail: the forename ELIAS runs in the Daubeney family as well as the Swonhunger one, which is what naming after a maternal line looks like.

rows.src: Ralph Bigland, Collections for Gloucestershire, volume 1 — read entire
rows.what: Every Saniger mention, not just the two already quoted here
rows.got: Twenty mentions. The Berkeley monuments record one household across four generations WITH AGES: Esther daughter of Edward Saniger buried 16 August 1692; Esther wife of Edward Saniger died 13 June 1693; EDWARD SANIGER OF SANIGER, GENT, buried 3 December 1739 AGED 48; SUSANNA his relict died 14 May 1744 AGED 58; JANE their daughter died 15 June 1750 AGED 24; and an EDWARD SANIGER SENIOR whose year is broken in the scan. Also «EDWARD SANIGER, OF PEDINGTON IN THIS PARISH» and Mary his wife — Peddington being one of the places named beside Swanhanger in the 1626 inquisition of Henry Mallett.

rows.what: Awre and Blakeney, the half of this family FreeREG cannot reach
rows.got: Nothing, and the null was already established at book level: Rudder contains NO Saniger under any spelling in 5.7 million characters, against a control of 804 Berkeley mentions and an index carrying Wanswell, Hamfallow, Halmore and Alkington. He mentions Awre 194 times and Blakeney 20, so the parishes are well covered — they simply hold nobody of this name in his account. Bigland, by contrast, gives twenty.

rows.what: All 67 digitised volumes, twelve spellings, each volume controlled by its own Berkeley mention count
rows.got: Sixty-seven attempted, ONE UNFETCHABLE and recorded as unread rather than empty, TWELVE carrying the name. The substantial ones are volume 6 (Cooke's «Wanswell Court»), volume 22 (the deeds in full translation), volume 10 (the Daubeney pedigree) and a fourth printing the chantry licence of 1356. The rest are membership lists and one unrelated pedigree using Sanigar as an address.

rows.src: TBGAS — the chantry of Our Lady at Stone, 1356
rows.what: Whether any Crown record of this date names the family
rows.got: One does, and it is a licence rather than an inquisition. John Sergeant of Stone endowed a chantry for a priest to pray «for the good estate of himself and of John Sergeunt his father and of Thomas Lord Berkeley and of Maurice Berkeley his son, AND OF WILLIAM SON OF WILLIAM SWANHANGRE, AND ALIENOR HIS MOTHER» — authorities Letters Patent 30 Edw. III pt 3 m.22, Fine Roll m.3, and the inquisition ad quod damnum. ALIENOR is a woman of this family named nowhere else read here. The Serjeants took the other half of the Stone inheritance and were still praying for the Swanhangres a generation after the partition.

rows.src: «William son of William Swanhangre» — an unresolved conflict
rows.what: Whether the chantry licence can be fitted to the line the Berkeley deeds give
rows.got: It cannot, not yet. BCM/A/1/24/184 of the same year, 1356, makes William the son of JOHN — «a charter of John Swonhungre, his father, son and heir of John Swonhungre». The chantry licence makes a William the son of a William, by a mother called Alienor. Either two Williams were living at once, which other deeds make plausible, or one source is wrong. Recorded as unresolved rather than reconciled.

rows.src: E 179 — the Tudor subsidies for BERKELEY hundred
rows.what: Whether named taxpayers survive between the medieval deeds and the parish registers
rows.got: Six pieces, all described as ASSESSMENT (INDIVIDUALS) — meaning named taxpayers, not just totals. E 179/114/240 (8 Nov 1543); E 179/114/235 and E 179/114/296/5 (both 1544–46); E 179/114/272 (6 March 1546, with Henbury and Barton Regis); E 179/114/295 (1549, the «relief»); E 179/115/307 (1549, county-wide). None digitised.

rows.src: E 179 — the Tudor subsidies for BLEDISLOE hundred
rows.what: The Forest side — Awre and Blakeney, which no other source reaches
rows.got: They survive, and they matter more than the Berkeley ones because nothing else covers these parishes. E 179/114/287/1, [1523–1525], «Assessment (individuals)»; E 179/114/252, [1524], St Briavels and Bledisloe, assessment of individuals; E 179/114/230, [1524]; E 179/113/204, 20 Dec 1524, certificate; E 179/114/287/2, [1544], assessment of individuals; E 179/114/246, 10 Oct 1544. **This archive has no Sanigers at Awre** — see correction 32 — so the Bledisloe pieces matter far less than the Berkeley ones. The point stands for BERKELEY hundred, where the muster found three men of the name.

rows.src: A published edition of the Gloucestershire subsidies
rows.what: Whether any of it can be read without going to Kew
rows.got: Not freely. Searches of the Internet Archive for «military survey Gloucestershire 1522», for a published 1524 subsidy roll, and for a separate edition of Men and Armour all return nothing. The Gloucestershire Record Series editions of this material are modern and in copyright. The catalogue descriptions are free; the names are not.

rows.what: Whether the archive's own contradiction detector could be made worth reading
rows.got: **31 flagged pairs became 14, and none of the three changes was «tighten the window».** A year is now attributed to ONE event rather than to every event nearby; of those, the event word BEFORE the year wins, because English writes «married 21 June 1779» and «baptised 19 March 1780»; and «married» now matches the abbreviation «m. », which «born» and «died» already matched and which was why the archive's own pedigree tables read as contradictions. The meta-registers — /worklist, /open-questions, /coverage, /errands, /corrections — joined the skip list, because a sentence EXPLAINING a false positive is indistinguishable from the false positive. That was noticed when the note written to explain the Joseph D'Arcy case became a fresh source for it.

rows.what: Whether «59 of 89 nulls name no control» was true
rows.got: It was not; it was too harsh, and the fault was in my detector rather than in the rows. It required a DIGIT, so it missed «John Smith across the WHOLE OF CHESHIRE for 1800–1820 returns TWO entries», «transcribed in full — 7,967 records, 1545–1903» and «Dursley runs to 1951 and Cam to 1939, so the window is well covered» — all of them controls, stated in words. Widening it then introduced the opposite fault: it accepted «1841 entries», where the number is a YEAR. The real count is 55 named and 39 unstated of 94. The lesson is that the detector was the wrong shape: `ctl` is now a FIELD the author sets, and the pattern survives only as the bootstrap that set it once.

rows.src: White's History, Gazetteer and Directory of Staffordshire, 1834 and 1851
rows.what: The Sneyds of Well Street, Hanley, in the years between censuses
rows.got: Neither man is there, and the reason is worth more than the search. SNEYD IS A STAFFORDSHIRE GENTRY NAME: of 63 mentions in the 1834 volume the overwhelming majority are the landed family — Basford Hall, Belmont, Ashcombe, Sneyd Green, the Rev. John Sneyd M.A., Thomas Sneyd Esq., the Misses Elizabeth and Harriot. A search on this surname in this county returns the gentry by default. Two TRADESMEN Sneyds do appear in 1834 with street addresses, SETH SNEYD of Oxford Street and RICHARD SNEYD of New Market Street, and neither is this archive's Samuel the grocer or James the engraver.

rows.src: White's Staffordshire — how far the control goes
rows.what: Whether the null is worth anything
rows.got: Only partly, and the limit is stated rather than hidden. The books are the right books — Hanley 51 mentions, Shelton 36, Piccadilly (a Hanley street) 45, «grocer» 86 — but «Well street» appears NOWHERE in either scan, and the 1851 volume's «engraver» entries are from the Birmingham end of the county, around Soho. The OCR of these two-and-a-half-megabyte directories is poor. So this is a null against a book whose street-by-street sections cannot be shown to be fully readable, which is weaker than the FreeREG nulls and is recorded as such.

rows.what: A digitised county directory that would carry Saniger clothiers and weavers
rows.got: None found free. The Internet Archive has White's for Staffordshire in two editions and Slater's and Pigot's national directories for Scotland, Manchester and 1878–86, but searches for a Gloucestershire or Bristol county directory of the right period return NOTHING. The Gloucestershire volumes are on subscription sites and at the University of Leicester's Special Collections. The Staffordshire half of this question could be asked; the Gloucestershire half could not.

rows.src: The atlas gazetteer, for the medieval hamlets
rows.what: Whether Saniger, Wanswell, Hinton, Awre and Blakeney can be put on the map
rows.got: Only two of the five honestly can. All five geocoded — but WANSWELL, HINTON and SANIGER returned the SAME coordinate, Berkeley's, and BLAKENEY returned AWRE's, every one of them stamped «exact» by a gazetteer that has simply never heard of the hamlets. Three pins on one point claiming exactness is worse than an omission, so only Saniger and Awre are shown, each saying in its own caption that the point is the PARISH and which neighbours share it.

rows.src: agree.py's PLACE half, read for the first time
rows.what: Whether the half of the tool nobody had triaged was saying anything
