rows.got: It was, and the fault was structural. **11 (person, event) pairs carried more than one place, and /sneyd supplied most of them** — a SURNAME AGGREGATION PAGE listing every Sneyd in the archive, so a proximity test read four men born in four places as one man born in four. It also put KEELE, seat of the Staffordshire gentry Sneyds, beside a Hanley grocer. Adding the surname pages to SKIP took it to **4**, and all four are explicable: Samuel Sneyd born Madeley and living at Hanley, and a George Pitt D'Arcy «born at Brisbane in 1864» who is the fourth man of that name, as the archive's own text says.

rows.src: crossread.py, run against the rewritten open questions
rows.what: Whether it finds anything the archive does not already know
rows.got: No finding, and the shape is the reason. It reads 903 files and prints, for each open question, every file that mentions the question's terms — a CONCORDANCE, not a detector. It reaches no verdict and flags no conflict, so its output is 900 files of co-occurrence for a reader to triage by hand. Controlled in the sense that it plainly ran and plainly matched: the parentage question returns families.json, register.json, ancestors.json and twenty more. **It needs the treatment agree.py had today, or retirement.**

rows.src: The coverage verdicts, read against the template that renders them
rows.what: Whether any verdict displays as something other than what it means
rows.got: Two did. The template was a FALLTHROUGH CHAIN — good, partial, absent, and everything else «cannot answer» — so **BLOCKED** (a source nobody has asked, because it wants an account this archive will not make) rendered as a source that had been asked and could not answer. And one row carried the freehand verdict «unusable as a control», which fell through the same way. The vocabulary is now declared in the data, the template looks it up instead of falling through, and a check refuses any verdict outside it.

rows.src: J. H. Cooke, «Wanswell Court» — read entire
rows.what: What the pages nobody had read do to the 1774 sentence
rows.got: They weaken it as independent testimony and strengthen it as a fact. Cooke names his source: «William Thorpe… married URSULA second daughter of JOHN SMYTH OF NIBLEY… TO WHOSE MS. HISTORY OF THE HUNDRED OF BERKELEY, STILL PRESERVED AT THE CASTLE, I AM INDEBTED FOR MOST OF THE FOREGOING PARTICULARS.» So the medieval descent is SMYTH'S, and this archive has partly been hearing Smyth twice. But Smyth died in 1641, so the 1774 sale cannot be his — it rests on the Wanswell title deeds Cooke cites elsewhere, or on the Lysons pamphlet. The footnote marker after «1774» survives in the scan; the note does not.

rows.src: Cooke on the descent of the MANOR, as against the hamlet
rows.what: Whether Saniger Farm and Wanswell are the same property
rows.got: They are not, and the archive had been asking the question badly. Wanswell went Thorpe (from 1402, ten generations) → **Daniel Lysons of Gloucester in 1672 for £3,500** → **Colonel Berkeley, afterwards EARL FITZHARDINGE, in 1818 for £25,769**, and «has ever since formed an integral portion of the Berkeley Castle estate». Saniger was OUTLYING LAND of that manor, sold off in parcels: Cooke prints a summons of 1638 to «William Jones, Esq., of Nasse, near Lydney, who had purchased of George Thorpe some outlying land AT SANIGER, part of the manor of Wanswell». So the 1774 sale is a separate, smaller transaction — and more plausible for it.

rows.src: Rev. D. Lysons, «Brief Historical Account of the Manor of Wanswell» (1817)
rows.what: A source named by Cooke and unknown to this archive
rows.got: «A quarto pamphlet of 6 pages, published in 1817, now very scarce», written by the family that had owned Wanswell since 1672, a year before they sold it, and quoting the abstract of title. Cooke uses it for the 1672 purchase price. It has not been sought.

rows.src: Cooke's date for George Thorpe's death
rows.what: Whether «went to Virginia, where he died in 1662» can be repeated
rows.got: It cannot. The George Thorpe of the Virginia Company was killed in the massacre of 1622, and Cooke's own narrative gives the 1672 sale of Wanswell to that man's SON, also George — a man who died in 1662 cannot be succeeded by a son selling ten years later while his father's widow still holds a life interest. **1662 is a misprint or misreading of 1622** and this archive will not repeat it.

rows.what: Where the family came from before it was named from Saniger
rows.got: **Esshelesworth is ASHLEWORTH**, a Gloucestershire parish on the Severn north of Gloucester, Domesday's *Escelesworde* — and the deeds hold the transaction that made the surname. BCM/A/1/24/67, late Henry III: «Maurice de Berkel' and THOMAS DE ASSHELWORTH… 7 acres of land in the MANOR OF HAMME, next to the road between the new ditch and Bradeflet; rent 2s. 11d. a year, and Thomas has given him one bezant.» The manor of Ham contains Swonhungre, and in the next reign a «Thomas de Swonhungre, son of Thomas de Esshelesworth» is dealing in the same parish. Graded inferred: nothing says the two Thomases are one man.

rows.src: The printed Calendars of Inquisitions Post Mortem, for RICHARD II
rows.what: Converting the regnal citations in the TBGAS pedigree to modern references
rows.got: Not possible from free sources. The digitised run on the Internet Archive is the 1898–1904 series covering Henry III to Edward III, plus one Henry VII volume; **the Richard II volumes were published in the twentieth century and are in copyright**. Discovery's C 136 series IS name-indexed — «C 136/82/12, 17 Rich II, William Wauton, knight: Essex» — but no Gloucestershire Wauton or Giffard inquisition surfaces under a plain search. So «16 Richard II part 1 no. 16» and «18 Richard II no. 81» cannot be converted to a modern piece reference from here.

rows.src: Discovery, for JOHN DE WYKE and the Kingsholm interest
rows.what: Alice's probable father, and the manor the Daubeney marriage brought in
rows.got: Almost nothing, against a catalogue that returns 195 records for the surname and itemises the Berkeley muniments deed by deed. «de Wyke» with Berkeley and Hamme returns five records, of which the only new one is BCM/A/1/24/23 of 1321 — «Denise widow of Richard de Wyke… 6¼ a. pasture called Cobyeslese by Wyke, in Hamme». No John de Wyke, and no medieval Kingsholm manor records at all. The Wykes are in the witness lists from the 1260s onward; they are simply not the subject of surviving deeds.

rows.src: Every external URL this archive cites
rows.what: Whether the sources it points at still resolve
rows.got: 566 distinct external URLs across the data files. **97 resolve, 429 redirect, 19 refuse a robot (401/403/429) and 21 did not answer** — and only those 21 are candidates for a dead citation. The first run of the tool reported «457 of 566 did not return 200» by counting redirects and door policies as losses, which is the cry-wolf shape that makes a report stop being read. A 3xx is a move and a 403 is a site refusing a machine, not a citation that has died.

rows.src: The medieval people, and whether they belong in the register
rows.what: A decision, not a search
rows.got: They belong, and /who settles it in its own words: «the people this archive met in documents and never had anywhere to put… They are in the record, and LEAVING THEM OUT WOULD BE EDITING IT.» Twenty-one are now in `build_register.py` with the deed that names each — Thomas de Asshelworth, four Stones including Juliana and Elyanora, Alice and Joan, John de Wyke, five wives, and the last John who died in 1401/2. The register rose to 381 record lines and the site to 875 pages. **None is claimed as a relative**, and /swonhungre still says in terms that no descent joins them to the Sanigers of the registers — that is a question about the tree, not about whether the archive admits what it read.

rows.what: Settlement examinations and removal orders for Berkeley — the record that names a labourer's parents and birthplace
rows.got: Not searchable by name, and the reason is structural. Discovery catalogues the **Gloucestershire Quarter Sessions as a single series** — «Q, 1660–2007» — and its item-level entries for the period are «Memoranda of convictions, general», bundle by bundle. Parish overseers' records sit in the P series at Gloucestershire Archives and are catalogued at bundle level too. A control shows what itemisation looks like when it exists: the same catalogue lists 195 records for this surname and describes every Berkeley Castle DEED individually. **The poor-law records are not indexed by name anywhere reachable**, so this is a visit, not a search.

rows.src: Berkeley Castle Muniments — the COURT ROLLS, as against the deeds
rows.what: The Ham manor court roll of 26 May 1600 that Cooke cites
rows.got: Not itemised. Discovery describes the BCM **deeds** one by one — that is where this archive's 195 records came from — but returns only the collection-level «BCM, 1153–17th cent» for court rolls, and nothing at all for a Ham or Hinton manor roll. Cooke read the roll of 26 May 42 Elizabeth in the 1880s and quoted the homage presenting Nicholas Thorpe's death; **the document exists and the catalogue does not reach it.**

rows.what: The earlier of the two partitions Cooke names
rows.got: Not found. Cooke says the sisters' lands «were subsequently divided by several deeds of partition in **1347 and 1353**»; TBGAS volume 22 prints the 1353 indenture entire. Searching the Berkeley catalogue for a Swonhongre partition naming Hasilcote, Kingscote or Nibley returns nothing, against a catalogue that itemises 178 BCM records under these spellings and gave up the 1353 deed, the 1354 Nibley partition and the 1356 inspeximus. **Either the 1347 deed is among the unitemised court rolls, or Cooke was counting the 1354 indenture as a second partition.**

rows.what: Whether this family is in Awre and Blakeney at all
rows.got: **It is not, and the premise was mine.** Volume 2 mentions **Awre 172 times and Blakeney 4** across 4.4 million characters, and names **no Saniger under any spelling** — while volume 1 gives twenty at Berkeley. Rudder mentions Awre 194 times and names none in the whole book. And the 1608 muster puts all eleven men at Halmore, Hinton and Saniger in Berkeley, at Wotton-under-Edge, Woodmancote, Dursley, Paganhill and three Stonehouse hamlets. **There is no Forest side of this family.** I wrote the phrase into a work-list note this morning and read it back all day as though a source had said it. Now correction 32.

rows.src: TBGAS volume 22 — whose deeds they are
rows.what: The numbered series printed in full translation
rows.got: «**Documents relating to the Monastery of St Mary Kingswood, belonging to Mr. F. F. FOX. Transcribed by Mr. V. R. PERKINS.**» **Forty-six numbered deeds**, in a private collection — a third body of muniments, separate from Berkeley Castle and from Smyth's own papers at Birmingham. Eleven mention this surname. Kingswood Abbey held land in the same parishes, which is why a Swonhungre partition is among them.

rows.src: Smyth's survey, read for BELLAMY'S PLACE
rows.what: The property whose two halves descended through both sisters until 1605
rows.got: Smyth gives the Stone descent independently, and it matches the deeds exactly: Bellamy's Place at Southend in Nibley «was anciently… the land of **ROBERT DE STONE, FATHER OF ROBERT DE STONE, FATHER OF THOMAS DE STONE**, who in the begininge of the raigne of kinge Edward the second **was in ward for the same to Thomas then lord Berkeley**». Three generations from a survey of about 1639, matching BCM/A/1/24/190 of about 1304, **neither depending on the other**. Smyth adds that Thomas was a MINOR IN WARD. And the tenure repeats: «the xvj[th] part of a knights fee, sute to his hundred Court of Berkeley from 3. weekes to 3. weekes» — the same sixteenth Cooke found for Wanswell in the court roll of 1600.

rows.src: Smyth's survey, for the Great Berkeley Law-suit
rows.what: The 15th-century dispute Cooke invokes to explain the Thorpes' castle-guard
rows.got: Not in volume 3 under that name: «law-suit» and «lawsuit» return nought across 1.29 million characters, against a volume mentioning Nibley 73 times and Thorpe 108. The Description of the Hundred is a survey of properties, not a narrative of the family's litigation — that belongs to the LIVES, which are volumes 1 and 2. Cooke's sentence remains this archive's only account of it.

rows.what: GEORGE PITT D'ARCY, died at Parramatta 22 July 1849
rows.got: Not there. The volume is 3.5 million characters with **122 obituary sections**, and it carries three D'Arcys — Samuel Darcy Dickson of Ballyma[curragh], «at an advanced age, D'Arcy Mahon, esq.», and an index entry «D'Arcy, J. S. 446» — so the magazine does print the name. It simply does not print his. A colonial death in July would in any case sit near the edge of the year's reporting.

rows.src: The Gentleman's Magazine — what can be reached at all
rows.what: Whether the 1805 and 1848 volumes can be opened for Constantine and Joseph
rows.got: Not from the Internet Archive. **120 identifiers were checked, one metadata record at a time**, because the search index stamps every volume «1731» — the series start — and only the per-item `year` field is true. Of the 120, the years present run 1738, 1748, 1780, 1789, 1795, 1807, 1812, 1816, 1817, 1819, 1823, 1827, 1828, 1829, 1830, 1832, 1834, 1838, 1840, 1841, 1847, **1849**, 1850 and onward. **Neither 1805 nor 1848 is among them.** Constantine died in May 1805 and Joseph in 1848, and the volumes that would carry them are not in this holding.

rows.src: Bristol Archives, P/St.P and J/D/2(j) — read in full
rows.what: The Swonhungre with two shops in Bristol Market, 1443
rows.got: «1. Thomas Dodde of Stapulton', Glos. 2. Richard Venables and JOHN SWONHUNGRE. Premises: **two shops with gardens in the Market**, between a garden which John Hoper now holds to east, and tenement of Thomas Parkehous to west, extending from the market to **Bastelane** behind. Three deeds attached.» He is a grantee, with a partner, of urban property — and the reference is a PARISH one, St Peter and St James, so the deeds reached the church as endowment. The family's only known Bristol connection is by marriage: Isabel Swonhunger married **John Thorpe, a burgess of Bristol**, in 1402. Forty years is one generation. **No document states any relationship** and this archive claims none.

rows.src: Discovery, for the SERJEANTS of Old Court and for PEDDINGTON
rows.what: The family that took the other half of the Stone inheritance, and the second Saniger household
rows.got: Almost nothing, and the reason is the catalogue's shape rather than the families'. «le Serjaunt» with Berkeley and Stone returns **five** records against 195 for this surname, and they are Berkeley deeds in which a Serjeant witnesses. A Peddington search drowns in five thousand generic Berkeley hits. **Discovery itemises the Berkeley Castle DEEDS and almost nothing else for this hundred** — no court rolls, no parish chest, no manorial surveys — so a family that leaves no deed of its own is invisible in it, however well documented Cooke says they are.

rows.src: «William son of William Swanhangre» — resolved, probably
rows.what: Whether the chantry licence of 1356 contradicts the Berkeley deeds of the same year
rows.got: Probably not: they are probably two men. BCM/A/1/36/24 leases Hinton land to «**THOMAS SON OF WILLIAM DE SWONHONGRE**, Maud his wife and John the younger their son», so a William had a son Thomas; the chantry gives that William a son William and a wife Alienor. The William of BCM/A/1/24/184 is a different household — son of John, brother and heir of Thomas of Wanswell. **Two men of one name living at once is this family's commonest pattern**: a Thomas in every generation and four Johns. Recorded as a resolution, not a proof — no deed says they are two, and nothing rules out one.

rows.what: Robert and Joseph D'Arcy in the last January of the war
rows.got: Both. «ROBERT D'ARCY, R. ENG.» appears three times in the brevet and seniority lists, each time beside the men he had been commissioned and promoted with — GEORGE BRIDGES and SAMUEL T. DICKENS, both entered «do.», and George W. Dixon of the Royal Artillery. The same volume carries «JOSEPH DARCY, ROY. ART.» and a «Lt. Col. D'Arcy, h.p.» the OCR will not let anyone attribute. Thirty D'Arcy hits in 1.8 million characters, in a scan bad enough that his exact rank cannot be read.

rows.src: The annual Army Lists, 1776–1815, on the Internet Archive
rows.what: Whether the run can be walked year by year at all
rows.got: It cannot. **120 Army List identifiers were checked one metadata record at a time** — the search index is unusable for years, the same fault as the Gentleman's Magazine — and **exactly ONE falls between 1776 and 1815**: the Monthly Army List for January 1815.
